claims.text: Superconducting behavior in high-entropy alloys is governed by local modulations in electron–phonon coupling arising from compositional-disorder-induced atomic-scale lattice distortions.
Atomic size mismatch creates local strain fields.
Local strain fields modify phonon spectra and electron–phonon coupling strength, thereby tuning Tc.
An equiatomic NbTiZrHfTa alloy is an example of a superconducting high-entropy-element alloy suitable for the proposed initial state.
Composition can be systematically altered to vary average atomic size mismatch while approximately maintaining average valence electron count.
Substitution with elements of different atomic radii introduces controlled lattice distortions.
The comparison is restricted to samples that remain single-phase solid solutions and are measured at low temperature under zero applied magnetic field.
X-ray diffraction and pair-distribution-function analysis can quantify the relevant lattice distortions.
Resistivity, magnetization, and specific-heat measurements can determine Tc.
Atomic-scale lattice distortions induce local strain fields that alter phonon modes.
Local lattice distortions modify the local phonon density of states and consequently change the electron–phonon coupling constant λ.
A moderate increase in strain may enhance λ and raise Tc.
Excessive strain may introduce pair-breaking scattering that suppresses superconductivity.
Relative to a minimal-mismatch baseline, a moderate increase in size mismatch will shift Tc, although the direction of the shift is not specified.
Increasing size mismatch beyond an optimal window will decrease Tc because excessive electron scattering disrupts Cooper-pair formation.
The baseline alloy has minimal atomic-size differences, minimal lattice distortion, and a known Tc.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloy remains a single-phase random solid solution.
Phase separation or nonmetallic behavior may change the mechanism controlling superconductivity.
The relationship between atomic size mismatch and Tc depends sensitively on alloy identity and mismatch magnitude because enhanced coupling competes with increased scattering.
A lack of any significant Tc trend, or a continuously increasing Tc without a downturn over the tested mismatch range, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
